newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa gets down to business in crime fight.
newsitem.headline: South Africa gets down to business in crime fight.

text.p: South Africa has called in a leading businessman to overhaul its troubled police force and ended a moratorium on police recruitment, winning near universal praise on Monday from business, politicians and the media.

But the tough Meyer Kahn, group chairman of South African Breweries (SAB), will have a battle on his hands to turn around a demotivated, inefficient and sometimes corrupt service so it can fight rampant violent crime, analysts said.
"Undeniably this is the most difficult job of my life," Kahn, whose two-year secondment to the police starts on August 1, told Monday's Citizen newspaper.

President Nelson Mandela has called in Kahn, who over three decades has built SAB into the world's fourth biggest brewer, to fill a new civilian position -- chief executive of the South African Police Service, SAPS.
Kahn said he would need all the aid he could muster to help police chief George Fivaz tackle some of the world's worst rates of armed robbery, murder, rape, car hijacking and burglary.
"I'll ask for help and support from everybody and anybody. I intend to start with the Almighty and work my way down."

Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, announcing the appointment on Saturday, said the aim was to relieve the much-criticised National Commissioner Fivaz of administration and bureaucracy so he could concentrate on catching criminals.
"As a civil service department SAPS is bound by often stifling regulations. Such red tape has reduced many management and crime-fighting initiatives to a snail's pace," Fivaz said.
"I welcome the opportunity to concentrate more on crime-fighting."
He said the overburdened courts also needed an overhaul to make sure criminals who got caught would be convicted.
Cynical South Africans have sneered as police announce one initiative after another but crime shows no tangible sign of abating, despite official statistics that things are improving.

But the announcement last week of an end to a three-year freeze on hiring new police has boosted morale in the 140,000-strong force that had hit a low through poor pay, understaffing, lack of resources and dangerous work.

And Kahn's appointment just a few days later has been hailed by the private sector as just about the best news yet in the fight against a crime wave that has hit business badly and left South Africa a far less attractive place for foreign investors.
"It is a bold and imaginative step," the South African Chamber of Business said.
"The appointment of Mr Kahn, coming so soon after the (lifting) of the moratorium of recruitment, will undoubtedly further strengthen both local and investor confidence."
A recent business survey showed crime was making many foreign firms rethink the extent of investment in South Africa.
Kahn said he knew he could not refuse when Mbeki suggested the job to him, saying "Your country needs you."
"His toughness as a manager is tempered by a common touch he has retained since his boyhood," Mbeki said.
"His mischievous humour and blunt style will no doubt make for a smooth entry into the police service."
The Star newspaper said on Monday in an editorial headed "Let the battle now begin" that Kahn faced an uphill struggle.
"Violent crime has torn this country apart. Let us hope there is now light at the end of the tunnel."
